name: Repetisjon av hele faget
intro: Det viktigste fra alle temaene samlet – fint å gå gjennom før tentamen og eksamen.
sammendrag:
English helps you communicate ideas, opinions and information in different situations. In this course, you practise grammar, writing, speaking, reading and analysing cultural expressions. You also learn to evaluate information and explore English-speaking countries and their histories.

## Passive, conditionals and reported speech

In an **active** sentence, the subject does the action; in a **passive** sentence, the focus is on what the action is done to. Form the passive with **be + past participle**. It is useful when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, and is common in news and science, but active sentences are often clearer.

**Conditionals** connect an if-clause with a main clause. The **zero conditional** describes something always true (present + present); the **first conditional** describes a real future possibility (present + will); the **second conditional** describes an unreal or unlikely situation now (past + would); and the **third conditional** describes an unreal past (had + past participle + would have). Do not use *would* in the if-clause: say “If I had money”. In formal English, use “If I were you”.

**Direct speech** repeats someone's exact words, while **reported speech** retells them. When the reporting verb is in the past, verbs usually move one step back in time, such as *will → would* and *is → was*. Pronouns and time expressions may change too. Reported questions use statement word order; yes/no questions use **if** or **whether**.

## Argumentative essays

An **argumentative essay** takes a position and supports it with logical arguments and evidence. Its introduction catches interest with a **hook**, gives background and ends with a clear **thesis statement**. Each body paragraph should develop one argument. The **PEEL** structure helps: make a point, give evidence, explain how it supports the point and link it to the thesis or the next idea.

Present a **counterargument** fairly, then **refute** it to show why your position is stronger. The conclusion summarises the main points and restates the thesis in new words; it should not introduce new arguments. Use a formal register, precise language and **linking words** to show addition, contrast, cause and effect, examples or conclusions. Support claims with evidence from reliable sources, identify those sources, and revise for structure, evidence, grammar, spelling and punctuation.

## Sources and reliability

Be **source-critical**: ask **who** made a text, **what** its purpose is, **when** it was published or updated, **where** it appeared, and **why** it should be trusted. Consider expertise, evidence and whether other reliable sources agree. **Bias** is a one-sided presentation and does not necessarily mean that every fact is false. **Fake news** presents false information as real news; shocking headlines, no named author and missing sources can be warning signs. **Clickbait** uses exaggerated headlines to attract clicks. Use **lateral reading** and fact-checking to check claims beyond the page itself.

When using sources, **quote** exact words with quotation marks and a reference, **paraphrase** ideas in your own words while still citing the source, or **summarise** the main points briefly. Use signal phrases and include a consistent list of references with details such as author, title, date and URL. Presenting someone else's work as your own is **plagiarism**. AI tools can help with ideas or language, but may give incorrect information or invent sources, so check their claims and be open about their use.

## Oral communication

Effective speaking is about communicating clearly, listening and keeping a conversation going, not having a perfect accent. In discussions, respond to others, build on their points, disagree politely and ask for clarification. **Follow-up questions** show that you are listening; **open questions** beginning with *why*, *how* or *what* invite longer answers than yes/no **closed questions**.

A presentation needs an introduction, a main part with a few points and examples, and a conclusion that sums up, thanks the audience and invites questions. **Signposting** phrases guide listeners through the talk. Use keyword notes rather than reading a full script; slides should support what you say. Speak slowly and clearly, stress important words and vary your intonation. **Fluency** means speaking smoothly without too many long pauses. Fillers such as “let me think” can give you time, and language should suit the situation.

## Young adult literature

**Young adult fiction (YA)** is written mainly for readers aged about 12–18, often with teenage main characters, though adults read it too. Common themes include identity, belonging, friendship, first love, family, independence, injustice, mental health, grief and loss. A **coming-of-age story** follows a character who grows and changes. YA includes realistic fiction, fantasy, science fiction and **dystopian fiction**, which depicts a frightening future society. First-person narration is common and can bring readers close to the narrator.

When reading, note characters and how they change, setting, narrator, important events and striking quotations. Consider what the story suggests about society and growing up. A **book review** gives basic details, a spoiler-free summary and an evaluation; an analysis can focus on key events, characters, themes and language, using quotations. Give a personal response and explain it. Write about story events in the **present tense** and connect the book to the world around you.

## Film, music and media

Films, music, games and other creative works are **cultural expressions** that can be analysed like literature. For films, consider genre, plot, characters and setting, as well as how film techniques shape meaning. A **close-up** can show emotion or detail; a **long shot** shows the setting; and a point-of-view shot shows what a character sees. Low and high camera angles can respectively make a character look powerful or small and weak. Soundtracks and sound effects create mood and tension; lighting, colours and editing also affect the experience.

When analysing a song, consider its **lyrics**, speaker, metaphors, repetition, rhyme and imagery. The repeated **chorus** often carries the main message. Explore how tempo, instruments and the singer's voice support the lyrics, and consider the song's context. Games can tell stories in which player choices change what happens. A **review** presents and evaluates a film, series, album or game, using examples and avoiding spoilers; it usually ends with a recommendation. English-language culture comes from many countries, not only the USA and the UK.

## Australia, New Zealand and Canada

Australia, New Zealand and Canada were colonised by Britain and are now independent democracies and members of the **Commonwealth**. They have elected parliaments and prime ministers, and all have histories of injustice towards Indigenous peoples. Each has worked in different ways on reconciliation and recognition of Indigenous rights and languages.

Australia is both a country and a continent. Its capital is Canberra; Sydney and Melbourne are its largest cities. Most people live on the coast, while the dry, sparsely populated interior is the **outback**. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived there for tens of thousands of years. Colonisation caused loss of land and the tragedy of the Stolen Generations. The country is now highly multicultural.

New Zealand's main islands are the North Island and South Island. Wellington is the capital and Auckland the largest city. Māori arrived from Polynesia before Europeans. The **Treaty of Waitangi**, made in 1840 between the British Crown and Māori chiefs, is regarded as a founding document, although its interpretation has been disputed. **Te reo Māori** is an official language, and Māori culture, including the haka, is visible in national life.

Canada's capital is Ottawa and its largest city is Toronto. It has ten provinces and three territories and is officially bilingual: English and French are official languages, with French the majority language in Quebec. Its Indigenous peoples are the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Canada describes itself as a cultural mosaic.

## Sammenhenger i faget

Grammar helps you express possibilities, report information and vary your writing. Essays, reviews and presentations all need clear structure, suitable language and examples, but they have different purposes. Source evaluation supports reliable arguments and responsible writing about books, media and society. Speaking and writing also connect: both require you to organise ideas for an audience. Literature and media can reveal perspectives on identity, culture and society, while knowledge of countries helps place those expressions in context.

## Huskeliste før prøven

- Choose active or passive voice to suit the focus; form the passive with **be + past participle**.
- Match the conditional form to the meaning, and do not put *would* in the if-clause.
- In reported speech, check verb tense, pronouns, time words and question word order.
- Make your thesis clear and develop one main argument in each body paragraph.
- Support claims with evidence, consider a counterargument and avoid new arguments in the conclusion.
- Check sources with the five questions; cite paraphrases as well as quotations.
- In discussions and presentations, listen, use signposting and speak clearly.
- Use present tense to write about stories and avoid spoilers in reviews.
- Explain how film or song techniques affect meaning, mood or the audience.
- Compare countries carefully, including shared histories and Indigenous peoples, languages and cultures.

quiz.text: Make the sentence passive: “Someone stole my bike.”
quiz.explain: was + past participle (stolen). We leave out “by someone” because it adds nothing.

quiz.text: Which conditional is this? “If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.”
quiz.explain: It describes a real possibility in the future: present + will.

quiz.text: How do you report the question “Do you like football?”
options: He asked do I like football.
He asked did I like football?
He asked that I like football.
He asked if I liked football.
quiz.explain: Reported yes/no questions use if/whether and normal statement word order.

options: One clear sentence that states your position
quiz.explain: The thesis statement tells the reader exactly what you are going to argue.

quiz.text: Why should you include a counterargument?
options: To show that you have considered other views and can refute them
quiz.explain: Answering a counterargument makes your own position more convincing.
A biased text may leave out information that does not support its view.

options: Copying a text word for word
Expressing someone's ideas in your own words
quiz.explain: Paraphrasing uses your own words, but you must still give the source.

options: Presenting someone else's work as your own
quiz.explain: Plagiarism is a serious form of cheating.

options: Why do you think the law should change?
quiz.explain: Open questions start with words like why, how and what, and invite longer answers.

quiz.text: What is signposting in a presentation?
options: Phrases that guide the audience through your talk
quiz.explain: Phrases like “Moving on to…” help the audience follow your structure.

options: A story where the main character grows up and changes
quiz.explain: The main character matures through experiences and challenges.

quiz.text: What should a book review avoid?
quiz.explain: A review should make readers curious, not reveal the big surprises.

quiz.text: What effect does a low camera angle often have?
quiz.explain: Looking up at someone makes them seem bigger and more powerful.

quiz.text: Why is context important when analysing a song?
options: It tells you the song's length
It helps explain what the song is reacting to
quiz.explain: Knowing when and why a song was made can explain its message.

quiz.text: What do Australia, New Zealand and Canada have in common?
options: They all have French as an official language
They are all republics with presidents
They were British colonies and are now democracies in the Commonwealth
quiz.explain: All three share British colonial roots and parliamentary democracy.

ekstra.text: The passive is formed with a form of “be” and the past participle.
ekstra.explain: Examples: is made, was built, has been sold.

ekstra.text: An argumentative essay only needs your opinion, not evidence.
ekstra.explain: Evidence makes arguments convincing. Opinions alone are weak.

ekstra.text: A text can be biased even if all the facts in it are true.
ekstra.explain: Bias can come from what is left out or how facts are presented.

options: Moving on to my second point…
ekstra.explain: “Moving on to…” tells the audience you are starting a new part.

ekstra.text: A good book review includes the writer's evaluation of the book.
ekstra.explain: A review tells the reader what you thought and why.

skriv.text: Rewrite “Someone stole my bike” in the passive voice, and explain when the passive is useful.
skriv.fasit: My bike was stolen. The passive is useful when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious.
kriterier: Forms the passive correctly with a form of be and a past participle.
Gives a valid reason for using the passive.

skriv.text: Report the sentence “I will call you tomorrow” using the reporting verb “He said”.
skriv.fasit: He said he would call me the next day.
kriterier: Changes will to would and tomorrow to the next day.

skriv.text: Explain how an argumentative essay can use evidence from a reliable source and respond to an opposing view.
skriv.fasit: The writer can use a fact or example from a reliable source and identify where it came from. The writer should present an opposing view fairly and then refute it with an explanation supported by evidence.
kriterier: Explains that evidence supports an argument and sources should be identified.
Explains that a counterargument is presented fairly and then refuted.

skriv.text: You find a shocking online article with no named author or sources. Explain how you would check whether its claim is trustworthy and how you could use its ideas in your own writing.
skriv.fasit: I would check who published it, its purpose and date, and whether reliable sources support the claim. I could use lateral reading or fact-checking. If I paraphrased an idea, I would still cite the source and include it in my reference list.
kriterier: Suggests checking the source and comparing the claim with reliable sources.
States that a paraphrase still needs a citation.

skriv.text: Explain one important difference between a book review and a film review, and one feature they should both have.
skriv.fasit: A book review can discuss the writing and language, while a film review can evaluate acting, visuals or sound. Both should evaluate the work with examples and avoid revealing important plot details.
kriterier: Gives a relevant difference between features of book and film reviews.
Identifies a shared feature, such as evaluation with examples or avoiding spoilers.

skriv.text: Describe how you could present an analysis of a song clearly to an audience, including one feature of the song you would analyse.
skriv.fasit: I would introduce the topic, use signposting to guide the audience through my main points, and finish with a summary. I could explain how the chorus carries the song's main message or how the music supports the lyrics.
kriterier: Includes a clear presentation structure or signposting.
Names a relevant song feature and explains what it can show.

skriv.text: Compare Australia, New Zealand and Canada by naming one feature they share and one difference between them.
skriv.fasit: All three were colonised by Britain and are now independent democracies in the Commonwealth. Canada is officially bilingual in English and French, while te reo Māori is an official language in New Zealand.
kriterier: Names a supported feature shared by all three countries.
Gives an accurate difference between at least two of them.

skriv.text: A student says, “If I would have more time, I will practise speaking English.” Rewrite the sentence as a second conditional and explain why that conditional fits.
skriv.fasit: If I had more time, I would practise speaking English. The second conditional describes an unreal or unlikely situation now, so it uses a past form in the if-clause and would in the main clause.
kriterier: Correctly uses past form in the if-clause and would in the main clause, without would in the if-clause.
Identifies the situation as unreal or unlikely now.
